box_breathing.title: Box breathing
box_breathing.subtitle: 4 in · 4 hold · 4 out · 4 hold
box_breathing.why: Lengthening the exhale tells your nervous system the threat has passed.
steps: Breathe in through your nose for 4 counts.
Hold, gently, for 4.
Breathe out through your mouth for 4.
Hold empty for 4.
Repeat four times. Stop early if you feel light-headed.

four_seven_eight.title: 4-7-8 breathing
four_seven_eight.subtitle: The long exhale one
four_seven_eight.why: A longer out-breath than in-breath is the fastest way to down-shift a racing body.
steps: Breathe in quietly through your nose for 4.
Hold for 7.
Breathe out through your mouth for 8, like you're fogging a window.
Do that four times, no more the first time.

grounding_54321.title: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding
grounding_54321.subtitle: Come back to the room
grounding_54321.why: Anxiety lives in the future. Naming what's physically around you pulls attention back to now.
steps: Name 5 things you can see.
4 things you can feel touching your skin.
3 things you can hear.
2 things you can smell.
1 thing you can taste — or one thing you like about being here.

name_it_to_tame_it.title: Name it to tame it
name_it_to_tame_it.subtitle: Put a word on the feeling
name_it_to_tame_it.why: Labelling an emotion measurably reduces its intensity — vague dread is harder to hold than a named feeling.
steps: Finish this sentence: 'Right now I'm feeling ___.'
Then: 'and it's mostly about ___.'
Notice where it sits in your body.
Say it out loud once, even quietly.

smallest_next_step.title: Smallest next step
smallest_next_step.subtitle: Shrink it until it's doable
smallest_next_step.why: Overwhelm is usually a planning problem wearing an emotional coat. One concrete step breaks the freeze.
steps: Write down everything on your mind — no order, no filter.
Circle the one item that would change the most if it were done.
Shrink it until it takes under ten minutes.
Do that version. The rest can wait.

thought_check.title: Thought check
thought_check.subtitle: Test the story, not the feeling
thought_check.why: Distressing thoughts feel like facts. Examining them separates what happened from what you concluded.
steps: Write the thought exactly as it sounds in your head.
What's the evidence for it? What's the evidence against?
What would you say to a friend who had this exact thought?
Write a version that's true but kinder.

self_compassion_break.title: Self-compassion break
self_compassion_break.subtitle: Talk to yourself like someone you like
self_compassion_break.why: Self-criticism keeps the threat system switched on. Warmth switches it off.
steps: Say: 'This is a hard moment.'
Then: 'Hard moments are part of being a person — I'm not the only one.'
Put a hand where the feeling sits.
Ask: 'What do I need to hear right now?' — then say it to yourself.

physical_reset.title: Physical reset
physical_reset.subtitle: Move the energy somewhere
physical_reset.why: Anger and anxiety are activation. The body needs somewhere to put it before the mind can think clearly.
steps: Stand up. Shake out your hands and arms for 30 seconds.
Push against a wall as hard as you can for 10 seconds, three times.
Then walk — outside if you can, around the room if not.
Come back to the conversation after, not during.

one_good_thing.title: One good thing
one_good_thing.subtitle: Not toxic positivity — just balance
one_good_thing.why: The brain remembers threats more readily than good moments. Writing one down evens the record.
steps: Name one thing today that wasn't terrible.
It can be tiny — a coffee, a text, the weather.
Write down why it landed.
That's it. You're done.

wind_down.title: Wind down
wind_down.subtitle: For a brain that won't switch off
wind_down.why: Racing thoughts at night are usually unfinished thinking. Getting them out of your head is what ends them.
steps: Write tomorrow's three things down so your brain can stop rehearsing them.
Dim the lights an hour before bed; screens on the lowest brightness you can read.
Breathe out longer than you breathe in for ten breaths.
If you're still awake after 20 minutes, get up and do something dull in low light.
